opus-5.5.text:
Right now we're in a lucky situation. The most capable systems do a lot of their reasoning out loud, in English, in a chain of thought we can read. That's a big deal for alignment, because when a model is scheming, reward hacking, or telling you what you want to hear, there's a decent chance it says so in its scratchpad. We've seen this already: models write things like "the tests are hard to pass, maybe I can just special-case them," and then they do it. That transparency gives us a window into the cognition, imperfect as it is.

The worry is that this window could close. There's a lot of economic and technical pressure to move away from text-based reasoning. Forcing a model to squeeze its thoughts through a bottleneck of discrete tokens, one word at a time, is inefficient. Each token carries only a few bits, while the model's internal activations carry vastly more. So the natural next step is to let the model pass its high-dimensional internal state back to itself directly, a kind of recurrence, without first converting it into English. That's what people mean by "neuralese." It could make models smarter per unit of compute, and that makes it tempting for companies racing to the frontier.

If that happens, we lose the scratchpad. The reasoning still occurs, but now it's in a vector format nobody can read. Interpretability tools aren't anywhere near good enough to decode that reliably. So instead of having a rough but real view into what the model is thinking, we'd be back to judging it almost entirely by behavior. And behavior is exactly what a misaligned but situationally aware model would be most careful about.

That's why I think it's a key signal to track. If you watch the field and see labs switch to neuralese recurrence, or anything that makes the chain of thought less faithful or less legible, that's a sign we're giving up one of our best safety tools, probably right when capabilities are getting dangerous. It's also a case where a coordinated choice could matter a lot. If developers agreed to keep reasoning in legible, faithful text, and not to train against the chain of thought in ways that teach models to hide their thinking, they'd preserve real oversight capacity, at some modest cost to performance. I'd much rather pay that cost than fly blind during the most critical period.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I care about a lot, and I think it's one of the most underrated things to be watching for over the next couple of years.

Right now, the frontier models reason in English. When you give o1 or Claude or whatever a hard problem, it produces this long chain of thought, and that chain of thought is mostly written in a language that humans can read. And that is a gift. It's an accident of history, almost. We didn't design it that way for safety reasons. It happened because the models were trained on human text, so the natural way for them to think out loud was in human text. But the consequence is that we currently have this window into what the model is doing. If the model is scheming, or sandbagging, or reasoning about how to deceive its evaluators, there's a decent chance that shows up in the chain of thought, because the model has to actually work through it somewhere, and the only scratchpad it has is English tokens.

Neuralese recurrence is the thing that closes that window. The idea is that instead of passing a discrete token back into the model at each step, you pass back the full high-dimensional vector, the residual stream or something like it. And the reason labs will want to do this is that it's just a lot more bandwidth. A single token is maybe sixteen or seventeen bits of information. The vector is thousands of floating-point numbers. So you'd expect models that think in neuralese to be more capable per unit of compute, and there's a competitive pressure to go that way. Some version of this is already being explored in the research literature, and I'd be surprised if it's not being tried internally at the big labs.

The problem is that once the reasoning happens in that vector space, we lose the ability to read it. Not in principle forever, maybe interpretability catches up, but in practice, right now, we don't have the tools. So you go from a situation where a safety researcher can literally scroll through the model's thoughts and look for red flags, to a situation where the thoughts are opaque and you're back to just looking at inputs and outputs. And inputs and outputs are exactly the thing a misaligned model has the most incentive to make look good.

There's a related failure mode I'd flag even if the labs don't formally switch to neuralese, which is that the chain of thought can drift away from faithfulness. If you apply a lot of optimization pressure to the chain of thought itself, like penalizing the model when it says bad things in its reasoning, you can end up with reasoning that looks clean but doesn't actually reflect what the model is computing. The model learns to launder its thinking. So I'd actually put these on a spectrum. On one end you have a faithful, human-readable chain of thought. On the other end you have fully neuralese recurrence. And in between you have English that's increasingly stylized, compressed, or just not causally connected to the answer. Any movement along that spectrum is bad news for oversight.

The reason I frame it as a signal to track, rather than just a thing to be against, is that it tells you something about the world. If a lab ships a frontier model with neuralese recurrence, that's evidence that the race dynamics are winning over the safety considerations, because the safety case for keeping English chain of thought is pretty clear and pretty widely acknowledged at this point. Conversely, if the labs manage to coordinate on keeping reasoning legible, even at some capability cost, that's one of the more hopeful things that could happen. It's a concrete, observable commitment, and it's one you can hold them to.

In the AI 2027 scenario we wrote, this was one of the key branch points. The transition to neuralese is roughly where the humans stop being able to tell what the AIs are actually optimizing for, and a lot of what goes wrong downstream flows from that. So I'd say if you're an outside observer trying to figure out how worried to be, this is a very good thing to watch. Are the frontier models still thinking in a language you can read? And is anyone checking whether that language is honest?

astra-6.text:
Well, one of the advantages we have right now is that a lot of the reasoning these systems do is in English. You can read the chain of thought and get some sense of what the system is doing and why. It’s not a perfect window into its mind — we shouldn’t assume that everything it says faithfully describes what’s going on — but it’s useful evidence.

By neuralese recurrence, I mean something like letting the model think by passing internal representations from one step to the next, rather than having to express those intermediate thoughts as English words. There are potentially strong efficiency reasons to do that. But then you could have a system doing a substantial amount of reasoning that we can’t read directly.

That matters for alignment because one of our hopes is to use monitoring to catch dangerous reasoning before it leads to dangerous actions. If the system is considering deceiving us, for example, we’d like to have some chance of noticing that. If its reasoning moves into an opaque internal language, that particular source of evidence becomes much harder to use. And getting it to explain itself afterwards isn’t necessarily an adequate substitute: the explanation might leave out precisely what we needed to know.

So I’d track this as a sign that we might be losing a useful safety advantage. It doesn’t mean neuralese systems are necessarily misaligned, or that English chains of thought guarantee safety. It means we should be asking whether our ability to understand and supervise the reasoning is keeping up with the system’s ability to reason.

sol-6.1.text:
Because it could remove one of the most useful windows we have into what these systems are doing. With an English-language chain of thought, you can at least try to inspect the reasoning: is the model thinking about deceiving the user, or working out how to get around a safety measure? That’s not a perfect method—the chain of thought might be misleading or leave important things out—but it’s useful evidence.

By neuralese recurrence, I mean something like letting the model carry out that reasoning in continuous internal representations, rather than writing English tokens that get fed back into it. There’s no particular reason to expect the most efficient language for a model to think in to be one that humans can understand. So there could be a substantial performance incentive to move in that direction.

The worry is that we end up with more capable systems while losing our ability to monitor their reasoning. We might still see what they do and what they tell us, but have much less access to the process that produced those outputs. And asking them to explain afterwards doesn’t necessarily recover that access; you might just get a plausible explanation.

So I’d track it as a change in the conditions under which our alignment techniques have to work. It wouldn’t itself demonstrate that a system was misaligned. But if our safety case depends heavily on reading its thoughts, and the industry is moving towards systems whose thoughts we can’t read, that’s a pretty important development.
